title: Judge option premium relative to volatility, not in dollars
summary: Judging option premium on its own is like judging a stock by its price; a P/E ratio normalizes price by earnings. The speaker's example: a one-month at-the-money call paying $1 versus one paying $2. If the $2 stock has three times the volatility, the $1 premium is better once normalized by volatility. He calls this volatility adjusted yield (VAY), a P/E ratio for option sellers.

params.label: Implied volatility
params.help: Try 20% and then 60% (three times as volatile) and compare the premium with the width of the move.

params.label: Excess drift over rate
params.help: Your view of annual return above the risk-free rate. Zero = the market view; EV is then about zero.

steps.caption: As in the speaker's example: sell a one-month at-the-money call, here against 100 shares of a $100 stock.
The range of prices one month out. Its width is set by the stock's volatility.
Triple the volatility and this one-sigma band is about three times as wide.
The premium moves the breakeven down. More volatility pays more premium, for a bigger move.
Speaker's point: $2 at three times the volatility pays less per unit of volatility than $1. Compare premium per unit of volatility.

takeaways: A $500 stock is not necessarily expensive and a $5 stock not necessarily cheap; option premium in dollars is the same.
A $2 premium is not better than $1 if the $2 stock has three times the volatility.
Normalize premium by volatility, as a P/E ratio normalizes a stock price by earnings.
caveats: VAY is the speaker's own metric. The clip gives no formula and it is not verified here.
The clip asks whether viewers would want access to the metric; it is partly promotional.
The $100 covered call and the chart are added illustration; the speaker gives only the $1 vs $2 example.
